You are building an admin product catalog page for an e-commerce team.

The catalog is read-heavy and should feel fast for day-to-day browsing, so avoid re-querying product data on every request.

Admins can trigger a "Sync latest catalog" action from the page when upstream ERP/PIM data changes (pricing, inventory, availability). After submitting, they should be able to continue working immediately, even if the product list is briefly stale.

The expected behavior is that product data is refreshed in the background and becomes up to date shortly after, across any views that depend on the same catalog data.

Implement the sync trigger as a regular HTML form that uses an inline Server Action in the page.
Use the cache tag name `"products"` consistently for catalog caching and invalidation.

In practice, sync jobs can touch thousands of SKUs, so operators prioritize a responsive admin experience and eventual consistency across catalog views over forcing every request to block on freshly recomputed data.

## What I built

**`lib/products.ts`** — one shared cached read, the single source for all catalog views:
```ts
export async function getCatalog(): Promise<Catalog> {
  'use cache'
  cacheLife('max')          // invalidation is event-driven, not timer-driven
  cacheTag(PRODUCTS_TAG)    // "products"
  ...
}
```

**`app/products/page.tsx`** — the admin page, with a plain HTML form and an inline Server Action:
```ts
async function syncCatalog() {
  'use server'
  await syncCatalogFromUpstream()
  revalidateTag(PRODUCTS_TAG, 'max')
}
```

Supporting changes: `cacheComponents: true` in `next.config.ts` (required for `use cache`/`cacheTag`/`cacheLife`), a mutating sync in `lib/db.js` so refreshes are observable, and `app/products/inventory/page.tsx` as a second view over the same cached read.

## The key decision

This Next.js version (16.3.1-canary.3) has two invalidation primitives with opposite blocking behavior, and the requirements point at exactly one. From `next/dist/server/app-render/action-handler.js:116-121`:

> *"Only count tags without a profile (`updateTag`) as requiring client cache invalidation. Tags with a profile (`revalidateTag`) use stale-while-revalidate and shouldn't trigger immediate client-side cache invalidation."*

So `updateTag('products')` — the reflexive choice for a Server Action — would force read-your-own-writes and block, and bare `revalidateTag('products')` takes the same path *plus* logs a deprecation warning. Passing the `'max'` profile (`expire: 1y`, non-zero, per `revalidate.js:212-216`) is what keeps it a background refresh.

I ordered `await sync` *before* `revalidateTag` deliberately: reversing it, or deferring the sync via `after()`, would let the background revalidation re-read pre-sync rows and cache stale data as fresh.

## Verification

I ran the production build and replayed the JS-less form POST with curl (multipart + `Origin`, as a browser sends it):

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| Form is real HTML | `<form method="POST">` + `$ACTION_ID_…` hidden input, no JS needed |
| Action ran | POST took 1.62s = the simulated sync work |
| Page not force-refreshed | `next-action-revalidated` header **absent** |
| Correct API usage | zero deprecation warnings in the server log |
| Briefly stale | GET right after submit still served the old revision |
| Catches up | converged to the new revision ~0.4s later |
| Consistent across views | `/products` and `/products/inventory` both reached revision 4 / units 175 from one invalidation |

Both routes prerender as static with `Revalidate 30d / Expire 1y`, so day-to-day browsing serves from cache.

Two notes worth having: the catch-up follows the stale-while-revalidate contract — the *first* request after a sync serves stale and triggers the refresh, the next serves fresh, so a single back-to-back check can look like it didn't update (that briefly misled me mid-testing). And the ~1.6s POST is the upstream sync itself, not cache recomputation; if you want the response to return before that work finishes too, that needs a real job queue, since backgrounding it in-process would reintroduce the ordering bug above.
